title: Computational irreducibility explains free will despite deterministic rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Computational irreducibility explains free will despite deterministic rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Computational irreducibility provides an explanation of how humans, even if they follow definite underlying rules, can meaningfully be said to have free will.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it leads to an explanation of how we as humans—even though we may follow definite underlying rules—can still in a meaningful way show free will.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 1, “The Foundations for a New Kind of Science”; section “An Outline of Basic Ideas” (from p. 1), p. 6. Scope: human behavior and the philosophical question of free will

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch01-09: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.04

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The assertion is a philosophical interpretation rather than a discriminating empirical claim. Data on human behavior or computational predictability cannot settle whether that behavior meaningfully constitutes free will.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: No empirical decision criterion follows without first choosing a philosophical definition of meaningful free will. Behavioral unpredictability could be measured, but it would not confirm freedom rather than deterministic complexity.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Unpredictability does not distinguish agency from deterministic irreducibility.

Free will is not operationally defined.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.05
discriminating power: 0.02
data adequacy: 0.05
operationalizability: 0.05
analysis feasibility: 0.05

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The statement links a formal property of some dynamical systems to a meaningful attribution of free will. No public dataset records that attribution in a way that would separate this story from other compatibilist stories. The claim can be argued and cannot be confirmed or refuted by observation or computation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The claim offers computational irreducibility as an account of free will. Free will, in the sense used here, has no measurement that would confirm this explanation or favor a rival compatibilist account.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Free will is a philosophical predicate without an agreed observable.

Every deterministic and irreducible human-scale process is compatible with the explanation and with its rivals.
